capturedPayload.title: A rising coin, a mostly cash account

visual.caption: Hypothetical case inputs — not a live market chart

capturedPayload.scenario:
A hypothetical account starts with $80,000 cash and a $20,000 Bitcoin position. Bitcoin then rises by 10%. No trades, deposits, withdrawals or fees occur during this interval. A friend says the account must also be up 10%. Work through the position value and the cash separately before judging that claim.

Follow the account through a second hypothetical interval: after the rise, the Bitcoin holding falls 10% from its new $22,000 value. Cash still earns nothing and no trade occurs. Compare the final account with both its original value and its peak. A classmate proposes selling enough Bitcoin at the peak to restore the original 20% allocation; treat that as a separate, fee-free worksheet, not an automatic simulator order. Keep those branches separate.

questions.prompt: What is the Bitcoin position worth after the rise?
questions.explanation: Multiply the $20,000 position by 1.10. The $2,000 gain belongs to the invested portion. A quoted percentage change describes the asset, not automatically every account that holds it.

questions.prompt: What is the return of the entire account in this case?
questions.explanation: Cash remains $80,000 and the position becomes $22,000, giving $102,000 total. Divide the $2,000 account gain by the original $100,000. That is 2%, before any costs excluded from this case.

questions.prompt: Which denominator gives the new Bitcoin allocation?
options: $102,000 total account value
$100,000 starting value
$22,000 position value
questions.explanation: The new weight is $22,000 divided by $102,000, approximately 21.57%. Using the original balance gives 22%, but that is not the current portfolio weight because total value changed.

questions.prompt: After the second 10% move down, what is the Bitcoin holding worth?
questions.explanation: Apply 0.90 to $22,000 to get $19,800. Equal opposite percentage moves use different bases, so they do not cancel and restore the original position value.

questions.prompt: What is the account worth after that second interval?
questions.explanation: Add unchanged $80,000 cash to the $19,800 holding. The account ends $200 below its original $100,000 despite the earlier asset rally.

questions.prompt: What is the account’s full-period return across both intervals?
questions.explanation: Divide the $200 loss by the original $100,000 account. The asset loses 1% across the sequence, but its original account weight was only 20%.

questions.prompt: At the $102,000 peak, what Bitcoin value equals a 20% target?
questions.explanation: Twenty percent of current $102,000 equity is $20,400. A $20,000 holding would be slightly below the target because the portfolio denominator has changed.

questions.prompt: In the separate fee-free rebalancing branch, how much Bitcoin value would be sold?
questions.explanation: Subtract the $20,400 target from the $22,000 holding. Selling $1,600 transfers value to cash and leaves equity unchanged when transaction fees are excluded.

questions.prompt: What is the decline from the $102,000 account peak to $99,800, approximately?
questions.explanation: The peak-to-current loss is $2,200. Divide by the $102,000 peak, rather than the original account balance, to obtain approximately 2.16%.

questions.prompt: Which statement distinguishes the two account branches accurately?
options: The price refresh automatically performs the rebalance
A 20% target guarantees a 20% account return
Rebalancing changes exposure through a separate order
questions.explanation: A price refresh only marks existing units. A rebalance changes units and cash through orders; choosing an allocation does not guarantee the resulting return.

capturedPayload.reflection: Why can an accurate asset return still produce a misleading account-return claim?
capturedPayload.reflectionGuide: Name the share of money exposed to the move, show the unchanged cash, and use starting account value for return. Distinguish that calculation from current allocation, which uses the new total.

capturedPayload.title: The unchanged-price round trip

visual.caption: Hypothetical case inputs — not a live market chart

capturedPayload.scenario:
You buy $1,000 of a hypothetical asset and later sell the same quantity at the same quote. Apply a 0.1% fee to each $1,000 transaction. There is no spread or slippage in this worksheet. The price chart is flat, but the cash ledger will not be. Work out the two separate charges before describing the result.

Repeat the same flat-price round trip five times as a separate worksheet. Each transaction still has $1,000 notional, the quote never moves, and only the 0.1% fee applies. Compare activity count with accumulated cost. Then identify what a small price gain would need to cover before the round trip becomes profitable. A flat chart does not imply an unchanged cash ledger.

questions.prompt: What is the fee on the $1,000 buy?
questions.explanation: A 0.1% fee is 0.001 times the trade value. Multiplying $1,000 by 0.001 gives $1. Converting a percentage to a decimal correctly matters before using any fee estimate.

questions.prompt: What is the net result of the flat-price round trip?
options: No gain or loss
A $1 gain
A $2 loss
questions.explanation: The buy debits $1,001 and the sale credits $999. Subtract the debit from the credit to obtain −$2. The asset made no price gain, but both fees affected the account.

questions.prompt: Would doubling the number of identical round trips remove that loss?
options: Yes; fees cancel each other
Yes; a flat price ensures break-even
No; it doubles these assumed fees
questions.explanation: Two identical round trips incur $4 of fees under these inputs. More activity alone does not create an edge. This case deliberately excludes other execution costs, so real-world costs could differ.

questions.prompt: What is total notional for one complete $1,000 buy and $1,000 sell?
questions.explanation: The buy and sale each count toward turnover, giving $2,000 total. Turnover measures traded notional, not equity earned or the final holding remaining.

questions.prompt: What net cash arrives from the unchanged-price $1,000 sale?
questions.explanation: Subtract the $1 sale fee from $1,000 gross proceeds. The buy fee is separate and must also be counted when reviewing the entire round trip.

questions.prompt: How many transactions occur across five of these round trips?
options: 5 transactions
20 transactions
10 transactions
questions.explanation: Each round trip includes one buy and one sell. Five completed pairs therefore contain ten fee-bearing transactions rather than only five.

questions.prompt: What total fee is charged across those five flat-price round trips?
questions.explanation: Ten transactions each cost $1, giving $10 total fees. The absence of price movement does not erase the accumulated costs of repeated activity.

questions.prompt: What combined gross price gain would cover those $10 fees exactly?
questions.explanation: Net result equals gross price gain minus costs. In this fixed-notional worksheet, a $10 gross gain covers the stated $10 charges without creating positive net profit.

questions.prompt: Does a fee-free hypothetical chart establish a fee-free execution ledger?
options: Yes; all flat charts imply zero costs
Yes; a plotted quote already includes every user fee
No; the transaction rules must also be checked
questions.explanation: A chart records prices, while an execution ledger records units, cash and applicable charges. The two must be combined before evaluating net performance.

questions.prompt: Which record would make this repeated-trading review reproducible?
options: Only the final asset symbol
Both transaction notionals and each fee
Only the count of profitable-looking charts
questions.explanation: Recording the buy and sell notionals and charges lets another reader reconstruct net cash. A chart or trade count alone does not identify the costs.

capturedPayload.reflection: What should your journal say when the chart is flat but equity is lower?
capturedPayload.reflectionGuide: Reconcile the two fee entries rather than blaming an unexplained price change. Mark the excluded spread and slippage assumptions so the worksheet is not mistaken for a complete real execution model.

capturedPayload.title: A snapshot has an observation time

visual.caption: Hypothetical case inputs — not a live market chart

capturedPayload.scenario:
A screen refreshes at 10:05 but shows a provider observation stamped 10:02. A different website displays a newer-looking number without a timestamp. All times are hypothetical. Before declaring one quote incorrect, distinguish when the page loaded from when the underlying price was observed, and check the asset identifier and currency.

Now the page is opened again at 10:08, but its provider observation still says 10:02. The displayed mark has not acquired a new observation merely because it was fetched again. A second page identifies the same asset in USD at 10:07. Compare the ages before comparing the prices. A cached quote may remain useful for a labelled valuation even when it is unsuitable for a claim about the current market.

questions.prompt: How old is the stated observation at the 10:05 refresh?
options: Five hours
Three minutes
Zero minutes
questions.explanation: Subtract 10:02 from 10:05 to get three minutes. Refreshing a page does not necessarily obtain a new market observation; it can display a cached provider response with an older timestamp.

questions.prompt: Which timestamp best describes the age of the quote itself?
options: The time your account was created
The provider observation time
Only the page refresh time
questions.explanation: The observation timestamp belongs to the price data. The loading timestamp describes the interface request. Both can be useful, but substituting the latter can make an old observation appear newly priced.

questions.prompt: What should be checked before comparing the other website’s number?
options: Only the website’s font size
Matching asset, currency, time and methodology
Only which number is larger
questions.explanation: Two plausible prices can refer to different currencies, timestamps or market sources. An identifier and methodology check helps make the comparison meaningful; a visual difference alone does not establish an error.

questions.prompt: At the later 10:08 page visit, how old is the unchanged 10:02 observation?
options: Six minutes
One minute
Zero minutes
questions.explanation: Subtract the observation time from the viewing time. Fetching the same mark again at 10:08 does not reset its underlying age to zero.

questions.prompt: How old is the second page’s 10:07 observation at 10:08?
options: Six minutes
Eight minutes
One minute
questions.explanation: The second observation was recorded one minute before viewing. Its age differs from the first page even though both are inspected at the same time.

questions.prompt: Which stored field should remain unchanged when the same observation is served again?
options: The price silently converted into a forecast
The original observation timestamp
The original observation rewritten to 10:08
questions.explanation: A cache read should preserve the source observation’s timestamp. The response can have a new fetch time without suggesting the underlying price was observed again.

questions.prompt: Can a six-minute-old observation alone establish the price at 10:08?
options: No; it establishes a mark observed at 10:02
Yes; every successful fetch is a current quote
Yes; caching freezes the real market
questions.explanation: The mark describes the supplied observation time. Markets may move between observations, so a successful cached response is not proof of the current price.

questions.prompt: What identifier check should precede this timestamp comparison?
options: Matching font and display precision only
Matching website refresh animation
The same provider asset and quote currency
questions.explanation: Even simultaneous observations are not comparable if they identify different instruments or currencies. Resolve identity and units before attributing a difference to freshness.

questions.prompt: Which label communicates the first page’s data most accurately at 10:08?
options: Verified execution available at this price
Provider snapshot observed 10:02, fetched 10:08
Real-time price observed 10:08
questions.explanation: The label separates quote observation from page retrieval. It describes the available snapshot without promising current data or execution at a particular venue.

questions.prompt: What would strengthen a claim that one of these feeds is incorrect?
options: Matched-identity, matched-time evidence and provider methodology
A price difference with no timestamps
A faster refresh icon
questions.explanation: A time-aligned comparison can narrow alternative explanations such as different observation windows. Price differences alone do not establish which data source is wrong.

capturedPayload.reflection: Write an honest freshness label for this screen.
capturedPayload.reflectionGuide: Say “page loaded at 10:05; quote observed at 10:02.” Avoid calling it a continuous tick feed. Mention the missing timestamp when describing the competing quote instead of assuming it is fresher.

capturedPayload.title: An ETF can overlap a stock you own

visual.caption: Hypothetical case inputs — not a live market chart

capturedPayload.scenario:
Your hypothetical $10,000 account holds $2,000 of stock A and $8,000 of an ETF. For this worksheet the ETF has a fixed 10% exposure to stock A. Ignore other assets, fees and changing weights. Although you see two account rows, part of both rows depends on the same company. Look through the fund rather than counting labels.

In a separate sensitivity worksheet, stock A falls 20% and every other ETF holding stays unchanged. Keep the ETF’s 10% A weight fixed for this calculation, with no fees or trades. Trace the direct holding and the indirect slice separately before adding their losses. The result is conditional on these assumptions; actual fund weights and other constituents can also change.

questions.prompt: How much indirect A exposure is inside the ETF?
questions.explanation: Ten percent of the $8,000 ETF position is $800 under the assumed fixed weight. A fund holding can contain exposure to an asset already held directly, even though it appears as another row.

questions.prompt: What is the combined direct and indirect A exposure?
questions.explanation: Add the $2,000 direct holding and $800 look-through exposure. The resulting $2,800 is 28% of this $10,000 account. Counting the ETF as completely unrelated would miss the overlap.

questions.prompt: Does owning two rows guarantee broad diversification?
options: No; underlying exposures can overlap
Yes; row count is the diversification measure
Yes; any ETF eliminates company risk
questions.explanation: Diversification depends on what the instruments expose you to, not just how many names are displayed. A fund may hold many securities, but its overlap with direct positions can still increase concentration.

questions.prompt: What percentage of the account is directly invested in A?
questions.explanation: The direct $2,000 A position divided by $10,000 equity is 20%. Indirect exposure must be considered separately before computing the combined company sensitivity.

questions.prompt: What percentage of account equity is indirectly exposed to A through the ETF?
questions.explanation: The ETF’s $800 A slice divided by $10,000 account equity is 8%. The fund’s own 10% holding weight is not the whole account’s indirect exposure.

questions.prompt: What is total account weight dependent on A under the stated look-through method?
questions.explanation: Add 20% direct and 8% indirect company exposure. Counting the ETF as unrelated merely because it is a second row would miss the overlap.

questions.prompt: How much does the direct A holding lose in the 20% decline branch?
questions.explanation: Apply the selected 20% decline to the direct $2,000 position. The resulting $400 loss excludes the additional A exposure inside the ETF.

questions.prompt: How much does the ETF’s A slice lose in this branch?
questions.explanation: Apply 20% to the ETF’s $800 A exposure. Other constituents are assumed unchanged, so this $160 loss is the ETF’s supplied contribution from A.

questions.prompt: What is the combined account loss due to this A-only move?
questions.explanation: Add the $400 direct loss and $160 indirect loss. The $560 total is 5.6% of account equity under the fixed-weight, other-assets-unchanged assumptions.

questions.prompt: What change would invalidate treating this sensitivity as a complete account forecast?
options: Only the ETF name remaining the same
Only two rows being visible
Other fund holdings or weights also moving
questions.explanation: The worksheet isolates one company and freezes other inputs. Actual changes in constituents, weights or costs require a broader calculation and cannot be inferred from this isolated branch.

capturedPayload.reflection: What fund information would you inspect beyond this worksheet?
capturedPayload.reflectionGuide: Check the actual holdings, weights and date of disclosure. The assumed 10% is not a live ETF fact. Look for sector and company overlap as well as the number of fund constituents.

capturedPayload.title: A good process can have a losing outcome

visual.caption: Hypothetical case inputs — not a live market chart

capturedPayload.scenario:
Two learners each make one hypothetical decision. One records evidence, exposure and a review condition, then loses $50. The other skips those steps and gains $50. A single result cannot tell you which process is repeatable. Evaluate what was known at decision time separately from the outcome that became visible later.

For a separate process check, use a three-item checklist: recorded evidence, recorded exposure and a recorded review condition. Learner A recorded all three; learner B recorded none. This checklist is not a validated skill score or proof of future profitability. Use it to identify documented versus missing steps, then decide how repeated observations could support a fairer comparison than one $50 outcome.

questions.prompt: Does the winning result prove the undocumented process was better?
options: Yes; every profitable decision is well reasoned
Yes; evidence matters only after a loss
No; one outcome cannot establish that
questions.explanation: An outcome is one observation produced under uncertainty. It can be favorable despite a weak process or unfavorable despite careful reasoning. Assessing the pre-decision evidence avoids judging everything through hindsight.

questions.prompt: What should a process review examine first?
options: Only the final profit color
Only whether a friend agreed afterward
The information and rules available before acting
questions.explanation: Review the dated thesis, exposure and decision criteria before adding later information. That preserves a fair account of what could reasonably have been considered and makes later changes to the thesis visible.

questions.prompt: What would help compare the methods over time?
options: Deleting the losing decision
Calling either method certain after one result
Consistent prospective records across more decisions
questions.explanation: A complete sequence of records can reveal repeated weaknesses or strengths better than a selected result. It still needs context and uncertainty; prospective documentation reduces retrospective storytelling and omitted failures.

questions.prompt: How many of the three defined documentation items did A record?
options: Zero
Three
One
questions.explanation: The case explicitly records evidence, exposure and a review condition for A. Counting those items measures documentation completeness under this narrow worksheet definition.

questions.prompt: How many of those defined documentation items did B record?
options: Zero
Three
One
questions.explanation: The case says B skipped the listed steps. That creates a documentation gap even though B’s one supplied outcome happened to be profitable.

questions.prompt: What outcome difference separates B’s +$50 from A’s −$50?
questions.explanation: Subtract −$50 from +$50 to obtain a $100 gap. This single dollar comparison describes outcomes without establishing which process is repeatable.

questions.prompt: Does A’s complete checklist prove the next decision will win?
options: Yes; a review condition eliminates uncertainty
No; documentation is not a profit guarantee
Yes; all recorded processes are profitable
questions.explanation: A documented process can make assumptions reviewable, but the supplied checklist does not remove uncertainty or validate future returns.

questions.prompt: Which record helps assess whether each learner followed their stated plan?
options: The original dated plan and the actual actions
Only the final profit number
Only the winner’s username
questions.explanation: Comparing a plan written before the outcome with the subsequent actions distinguishes adherence from a story reconstructed after the result.

questions.prompt: What would make a repeated comparison more informative?
options: Selecting only the best decision from each learner
Changing the checklist to fit each outcome
Consistent inclusion rules, comparable exposure and costs
questions.explanation: Comparable records and predefined inclusion reduce selective interpretation. Exposure and costs affect outcomes, so a fair comparison requires more than repeating profit headlines.

questions.prompt: What feedback matches A’s single losing case without overclaiming?
options: The loss proves A should double the next position
The documented steps can be reviewed separately from the loss
The loss proves all three steps were useless
questions.explanation: The case permits a review of evidence, exposure and conditions independently of one outcome. It does not justify discarding the process or increasing risk automatically.

capturedPayload.reflection: How would you review the losing decision without automatically calling it foolish?
capturedPayload.reflectionGuide: Compare the planned reasoning with the evidence available then, note execution and costs, and identify what changed. Keep the loss in the record while avoiding a claim that good preparation guarantees success.

capturedPayload.title: Two unequal positions fall together

visual.caption: Hypothetical case inputs — not a live market chart

capturedPayload.scenario:
Consider $60,000 cash, $30,000 in a stock and $10,000 in a crypto asset. The stock falls 5% while the crypto falls 20%. Treat these as simultaneous hypothetical moves with no trades or fees. Both position losses matter, but averaging the two percentage changes ignores how much money was invested in each.

After the simultaneous declines, consider a follow-up interval: the stock rebounds 5% from its reduced value while crypto rebounds 20% from its reduced value. Cash stays unchanged. Prepare an account-value bridge showing both invested contributions and cash. These selected moves are worksheet inputs, not forecasts. Distinguish each holding’s own return from its contribution to the starting account, and check whether the two rebounds restore the original total.

questions.prompt: How much does the stock position lose?
questions.explanation: The loss is $30,000 multiplied by 0.05, or $1,500. A price move must be applied to the dollars held in that asset; it is not applied to cash or to another position.

questions.prompt: What is the combined account loss?
questions.explanation: The crypto loses $10,000 × 20% = $2,000. Add the $1,500 stock loss to obtain $3,500. The account becomes $96,500, so its return is −3.5% under the stated assumptions.

questions.prompt: Why is a simple average of −5% and −20% unsuitable here?
options: Cash must lose 12.5% too
Losses cannot be added
The positions have different dollar weights
questions.explanation: A simple average assumes equal exposure to the two assets and omits cash. Dollar-weighted changes preserve the different position sizes. Neither asset volatility nor the number of holdings alone supplies the missing weights.

questions.prompt: How much does the crypto holding lose in the first interval?
questions.explanation: Twenty percent of the $10,000 crypto position is $2,000. Applying that percentage to the stock position or the whole account would use the wrong exposure.

questions.prompt: What is total equity immediately after both initial declines?
questions.explanation: The stock becomes $28,500 and crypto becomes $8,000. Add $60,000 cash to obtain $96,500, a $3,500 account loss.

questions.prompt: What contribution does the stock loss make to starting-account return?
options: −5 percentage points
−30 percentage points
−1.5 percentage points
questions.explanation: The stock loses $1,500 on a $100,000 starting account. Its own return is −5%, but its contribution to whole-account return is −1.5 percentage points.

questions.prompt: What is the stock value after its separate 5% rebound?
questions.explanation: Apply 1.05 to $28,500, giving $29,925. The rebound starts from a smaller base than the original decline and therefore does not fully reverse it.

questions.prompt: What is the crypto value after its separate 20% rebound?
questions.explanation: Multiply the reduced $8,000 position by 1.20. The $1,600 rebound is smaller than the earlier $2,000 loss because the percentage denominator changed.

questions.prompt: What is final account equity after both stated rebounds?
questions.explanation: Add $60,000 cash, $29,925 stock and $9,600 crypto. The account is still $475 below its original value despite both holdings’ positive second intervals.

questions.prompt: Which comparison describes the initial dollar loss contributions correctly?
options: Both lost equally because both prices fell
Crypto lost more dollars despite the smaller position
Stock lost more because its position was larger
questions.explanation: Crypto lost $2,000 and stock lost $1,500. Dollar impact depends on position size and percentage move together, rather than either one considered alone.

capturedPayload.reflection: Explain which position contributed more to the loss and why.
capturedPayload.reflectionGuide: The smaller crypto position lost $2,000, exceeding the stock’s $1,500 loss because its assumed decline was much larger. Discuss both size and price change rather than treating either factor as the whole explanation.

capturedPayload.title: A sale fee uses the exit value

visual.caption: Hypothetical case inputs — not a live market chart

capturedPayload.scenario:
A hypothetical position was bought for $2,000 before its buy fee. Its market value is now $2,200 and you sell it all. Use a 0.1% fee on each transaction’s actual notional value. The sale fee is based on $2,200, not on the original $2,000 purchase or on the $200 gross price gain.

Assume the full position is sold at the stated $2,200 value and no other account activity occurs. Build a cash bridge from original purchase debit to net proceeds. Then test a separate exit at $1,800 using the same fee rate. Treat the two exits as alternative branches, not consecutive sales of the same holding. The fee depends on each branch’s actual exit value.

questions.prompt: What is the sale fee under the stated rule?
questions.explanation: Multiply the $2,200 exit notional by 0.001. That gives $2.20. A fee on the transaction’s whole value differs from a tax or charge calculated only on profit.

questions.prompt: What net sale proceeds reach cash?
questions.explanation: Subtract the $2.20 sale fee from $2,200 gross proceeds. The $2,197.80 cash credit contains original capital and gain. It should not all be reported as profit.

questions.prompt: What is the net gain after the $2 buy fee and sale fee?
questions.explanation: The original cash debit was $2,002. Compare it with $2,197.80 net proceeds to get $195.80. Both fee bases are their respective trade values, and each fee is counted once.

questions.prompt: What initial cash outlay includes the $2,000 purchase and its fee?
questions.explanation: The purchase fee is $2,000 times 0.001, or $2. Add it to the purchase notional to obtain the full $2,002 entry debit.

questions.prompt: What gross price gain occurs at the $2,200 exit before any fees?
questions.explanation: Subtract original $2,000 purchase notional from $2,200 sale notional. This price-only gain has not yet accounted for either transaction charge.

questions.prompt: What is the sum of entry and exit fees in the $2,200 branch?
questions.explanation: The entry charge is $2 and the exit charge is $2.20. Add both to obtain $4.20 total, rather than counting only the latest transaction.

questions.prompt: What is net return on the $2,002 initial outlay, approximately?
questions.explanation: Divide the $195.80 net gain by $2,002 total entry debit. The denominator includes the buy fee because this comparison uses actual initial cash spent.

questions.prompt: In the separate $1,800 exit branch, what fee applies to the sale?
questions.explanation: Charge 0.1% to the actual $1,800 exit value. The fee is neither based on the original purchase nor only on the position’s $200 loss.

questions.prompt: In that $1,800 branch, what is the net loss including both fees?
questions.explanation: Net proceeds are $1,798.20 compared with $2,002 initial outlay. Their difference is a $203.80 loss, including the entry and exit fees.

questions.prompt: Why must the two alternative exit branches be kept separate?
options: One position cannot be sold in full twice without another purchase
Both branches automatically occur on refresh
The fee changes the number of holdings into two
questions.explanation: Each branch imagines a different full-sale price for the same starting holding. Combining both as actual proceeds would double-count quantity and cash.

capturedPayload.reflection: How would you explain the difference between gross gain and net gain?
capturedPayload.reflectionGuide: Show the $200 price gain and subtract the $2 purchase fee plus $2.20 exit fee. Keep these expenses separate from the sale proceeds so the account ledger stays easy to verify.

capturedPayload.title: An aggregate is not one exchange’s last trade

visual.caption: Hypothetical case inputs — not a live market chart

capturedPayload.scenario:
A hypothetical asset trades at $100 on venue A and $102 on venue B. A provider reports an aggregate $101 reference. No volume weights or exclusion rules have been supplied. These three numbers can describe different measurements at the same time. A paper-trading mark also does not promise execution at any of these real venues.

Consider two possible aggregation methods as conceptual examples: equal weighting of $100 and $102, or 75% weight on A and 25% on B. Neither is asserted to be the actual provider method. Calculate both references and compare them with observed venue trades. The exercise distinguishes a calculated mark, a venue observation and an executable bid or ask.

questions.prompt: Does the $101 reference prove a trade occurred at exactly $101?
options: No; a reference can combine observations
Yes; every aggregate is a last trade
Yes; a midpoint is always executable
questions.explanation: An aggregate can summarize multiple market observations without being the price of a particular transaction. To describe a last trade, you need the actual venue, transaction and timestamp rather than only a reference figure.

questions.prompt: Can you recover the provider’s weighting method from these numbers alone?
options: No; methodology and input weights are missing
Yes; all aggregates are equal-weight averages
Yes; the larger venue price has full weight
questions.explanation: The stated reference happens to lie between the two inputs, but that does not reveal weighting, filtering or source coverage. Consult the methodology instead of inventing an algorithm from a single result.

questions.prompt: What does the simulator’s mark establish?
options: A valuation input for the paper account
A reserved real exchange fill
A guaranteed price for unlimited quantity
questions.explanation: A mark supports simulated valuation under the product’s rules. Real execution depends on an actual venue and available liquidity. Treat the provider number as a reference rather than a promise that money can be exchanged at that price.

questions.prompt: What reference does equal weighting of the two venue prices produce?
questions.explanation: Average the two supplied prices with equal weights: half of $100 plus half of $102 is $101. This matches the reported reference under one possible method.

questions.prompt: What reference results from 75% A and 25% B weights?
questions.explanation: Multiply $100 by 0.75 and $102 by 0.25, then add $75 and $25.50. The resulting $100.50 shows how different weights alter an aggregate.

questions.prompt: Does matching the equal-weight calculation prove the provider used that method?
options: No; several methods or inputs could produce $101
Yes; one arithmetic match proves the entire methodology
Yes; every aggregate must use equal weights
questions.explanation: A numerical match does not uniquely identify how a provider produced its reference. Additional observations or the published method are needed to establish the process.

questions.prompt: What is venue B’s price premium over venue A in percentage terms?
questions.explanation: Divide the $2 difference by venue A’s $100 price. The 2% relative gap should be labelled with its comparison base rather than treated as an account return.

questions.prompt: Does a calculated $100.50 reference imply a venue trade at that exact price?
options: Yes; it proves A’s $100 trade never occurred
No; a weighted reference can lie between venue observations
Yes; every reference is a recorded transaction
questions.explanation: A calculation can combine separate observations into a new reference value. That reference is not automatically evidence of an executed trade at the calculated price.

questions.prompt: Which additional data would be necessary to assess immediate execution?
options: Current venue bids, asks and relevant execution constraints
Only the aggregate reference
Only the arithmetic midpoint
questions.explanation: Execution depends on available orders and venue conditions. A reference price alone does not establish a bid or ask at which the user can actually transact.

questions.prompt: Which report keeps the hypothetical aggregation methods honest?
options: Attribute both to the provider as facts
Call the larger reference a guaranteed sale price
Label both weight choices as conceptual alternatives
questions.explanation: The case supplies alternative worksheet weights, not verified provider rules. Clear labels prevent a mathematical example from turning into an unsupported methodology claim.

capturedPayload.reflectionGuide: Label each source and timestamp, explain that their methodologies can differ, and compare like currencies. Acknowledge that this case omits volume weights and does not model real exchange execution.

capturedPayload.title: Correlation can change when you need it

visual.caption: Hypothetical case inputs — not a live market chart

capturedPayload.scenario:
Two hypothetical assets moved in opposite directions in three earlier observations. In a fourth observation both fall. A learner calls the fourth pair impossible because the assets were “uncorrelated.” The small sample cannot establish a permanent relationship, and low historical correlation does not promise that losses will offset in every interval.

Add the following hypothetical paired percentage moves: first observation A +2%, B −1%; second A −2%, B +1%; third A +1%, B −0.5%; fourth A −3%, B −4%. Treat them as a tiny illustrative sample rather than a permanent relationship estimate. Compare the direction pairs, then test an equal-dollar $1,000 holding in each asset for the fourth observation only.

questions.prompt: Does three earlier observations establish a permanent correlation?
options: Yes; three is always enough
Yes; opposite moves guarantee independence
No; the sample and period are limited
questions.explanation: Correlation is a sample-dependent statistic, not a fixed contract between assets. Three observations supply very little evidence, and a relationship estimated in one period may not hold in another.

questions.prompt: Can low past correlation guarantee no simultaneous losses?
options: Yes; simultaneous losses violate the definition
Yes; one asset must rise every day
No; individual intervals can still move together
questions.explanation: A low aggregate relationship can coexist with particular intervals where both assets fall. Correlation does not promise a hedge on every date, and changing conditions can alter the estimated relationship.

questions.prompt: What is the better way to describe the earlier evidence?
options: A guaranteed hedge
Proof of market-neutral profits
A limited historical pattern, with its sample stated
questions.explanation: Specify the period, observations and method used. Avoid upgrading a historical estimate into a guarantee. Even a designed hedge can retain mismatch, liquidity and cost risks beyond the correlation statistic.

questions.prompt: In how many of the four supplied observations do the assets move in opposite directions?
options: One observation
Three observations
Four observations
questions.explanation: The first three pairs have opposite signs while the fourth has two negative signs. Counting directions describes this sample without establishing a stable correlation coefficient.

questions.prompt: In the fourth observation, how much does a $1,000 A holding lose?
questions.explanation: Apply A’s selected 3% decline to $1,000 exposure. The $30 loss is a dollar contribution for this one observation, not the asset’s permanent risk.

questions.prompt: In that fourth observation, how much does a $1,000 B holding lose?
questions.explanation: Apply B’s selected 4% decline to $1,000. Its $40 loss joins the A loss rather than offsetting it in this particular same-direction observation.

questions.prompt: What is the combined fourth-observation loss on the equal-dollar holdings?
questions.explanation: Add $30 A loss and $40 B loss. Equal notionals do not force opposing performance when both supplied asset moves are negative.

questions.prompt: What return does that combined $2,000 position show for the fourth observation?
questions.explanation: Divide the $70 loss by the combined $2,000 starting value. Adding the two asset percentage declines without weighting would overstate the portfolio percentage.

questions.prompt: Do these direction counts alone supply a reliable long-run correlation estimate?
options: Yes; three opposite pairs guarantee permanent negative correlation
Yes; one same-direction pair proves permanent positive correlation
No; magnitudes, a suitable sample and method matter
questions.explanation: A small selected sample and sign counts cannot establish a durable statistical relationship. A defined method and broader representative observations are needed.

questions.prompt: Which statement is supported without overstating the evidence?
options: The fourth observation could not occur
Opposite earlier moves did not prevent a simultaneous loss in the fourth case
Diversification never helps
questions.explanation: The supplied pairs demonstrate that an earlier pattern did not hold in one later observation. They do not settle all diversification outcomes or future relationships.

capturedPayload.reflection: Write a diversification claim that acknowledges this limit.
capturedPayload.reflectionGuide: State that different exposures may reduce concentration but can still lose together. Identify the historical sample and avoid promising that one position will always offset another.

capturedPayload.title: Write the thesis before the price moves

visual.caption: Hypothetical case inputs — not a live market chart

capturedPayload.scenario:
A learner buys a hypothetical stock at $40, then sees it rise to $44. Afterward they write that a strong report made the rise obvious, although their original reason was a chart pattern. The revised story hides what was actually tested. A dated pre-decision note lets you compare the original hypothesis with the later evidence.

Assume ten units were bought at $40 and later marked at $44, excluding fees. Keep the original dated chart-pattern note and add the later report as new information rather than overwriting the first thesis. Compare the price gain with evidence about why the decision was made. A profitable result is compatible with weak attribution, so the journal should preserve the information available at each time.

questions.prompt: What is the observed price change in this case?
questions.explanation: The $4 increase divided by the $40 starting price is 10%. That observed return is separate from why the learner acted and does not validate a reason invented after the movement.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with replacing the original reason after the rise?
options: It makes the report a proven cause
It prevents a fair test of the original hypothesis
It improves the historical evidence
questions.explanation: A rewritten explanation can make outcomes look more predictable than they were. Preserve the original thesis and add new information as a dated update rather than silently changing what the decision supposedly tested.

questions.prompt: What should a useful pre-decision note contain?
options: Only the hoped-for profit
Evidence, uncertainty and a review condition
A certainty claim about the next quote
questions.explanation: A brief note can state the observable evidence, alternative explanations and what would prompt reconsideration. It creates a reviewable process without pretending a future price is known.

questions.prompt: What notional was invested in the ten units at $40?
questions.explanation: Ten units multiplied by the original $40 quote gives $400 before fees. This is the invested notional, not the total size of an unspecified account.

questions.prompt: What is the later ten-unit holding worth at $44?
questions.explanation: Multiply ten unchanged units by the later $44 mark. The $440 value can be verified without accepting any particular explanation of the price increase.

questions.prompt: What is the holding’s gross dollar gain?
questions.explanation: Subtract $400 original notional from $440 marked value. Ten units translate the $4 per-unit price move into a $40 position gain.

questions.prompt: What is the quote’s return from $40 to $44?
questions.explanation: Divide the $4 quote increase by the $40 starting quote. This 10% gross asset return does not establish how much an entire account earned after costs.

questions.prompt: How should the later report be recorded without changing the original thesis?
options: As proof the original note always mentioned it
By deleting the chart-pattern reason
As dated new evidence beside the original note
questions.explanation: A dated addition preserves which evidence was available when the decision occurred. Overwriting the entry note hides the hypothesis actually tested.

questions.prompt: Does the $40 gain prove the later report caused the price move?
options: Yes; journals determine market prices
No; the case supplies no causal test
Yes; every positive result validates the latest story
questions.explanation: The arithmetic establishes a gain but not its cause. Attribution requires evidence connecting the event and price response beyond an after-the-fact explanation.

questions.prompt: What comparison would best reveal hindsight rewriting?
options: The original note against the later revised explanation
Only the final green return badge
Only another user’s account rank
questions.explanation: A preserved original record exposes which reasons changed after the outcome. This comparison supports process learning without requiring a confident market forecast.

capturedPayload.reflection: Draft a pre-decision note for this case using only the supplied facts.
capturedPayload.reflectionGuide: You can state the hypothetical entry and acknowledge that no actual report evidence is supplied. Name information to investigate and a review condition; avoid inventing a catalyst to explain the observed gain.

capturedPayload.title: Cash after a fee-paying buy

visual.caption: Hypothetical case inputs — not a live market chart

capturedPayload.scenario:
A virtual account has $10,000 cash. You plan to buy 20 shares at a fixed $100 quote. For this worksheet use TradeHQ’s 0.1% fee on the $2,000 trade value. The quote stays unchanged afterward. Separate cash spent, the marked position value, and the fee: the fee is not a share that remains in the account.

Continue after the purchase: the 20 shares rise from $100 to $110 each, then all are sold at that exact quote. Apply the same 0.1% fee to the sale. There are no further cash flows or costs. Make a ledger showing original cash, purchase debit, remaining cash, gross sale proceeds and exit fee. Compare the gross price gain with the final net account gain; a gain in the asset and a gain in the entire account use different denominators.

questions.prompt: What is the total cash debit for this purchase?
questions.explanation: Twenty shares at $100 have a $2,000 notional value. The fee is $2,000 × 0.001 = $2, so cash falls by $2,002. Counting only share cost would leave the cash ledger overstated.

questions.prompt: What cash remains after that debit?
questions.explanation: Subtract the full $2,002 debit from $10,000. The resulting $7,998 cash plus $2,000 of shares equals $9,998 in equity at the unchanged mark; the $2 difference is the fee.

questions.prompt: Is the unchanged quote enough to keep total equity at $10,000?
options: No; equity is $7,998
No; equity is $9,998 after the fee
Yes; fees become holdings
questions.explanation: An unchanged asset price does not refund transaction costs. The marked holding still has $2,000 of value, but $2 has left cash. Equity includes cash and holdings, not the cash balance alone.

questions.prompt: What purchase fee is included in the original $2,002 debit?
questions.explanation: Convert 0.1% to 0.001 and multiply by the $2,000 notional. The $2 charge is an expense, not additional value held as shares.

questions.prompt: How many shares are owned immediately after this fee-paying purchase?
options: 20.02 shares
19.98 shares
20 shares
questions.explanation: The order buys exactly 20 shares and charges its fee separately in cash. A cash fee affects equity but does not silently alter the order quantity.

questions.prompt: At the later $110 quote, what is the position’s marked value?
questions.explanation: Twenty shares multiplied by $110 gives $2,200. Purchase fees affect net performance, but are not added to the current units-times-quote valuation.

questions.prompt: What exit fee applies to the $2,200 sale?
questions.explanation: Multiply the $2,200 sale notional by 0.001. Reusing the original $2 purchase fee would understate the charge on this larger exit value.

questions.prompt: What is final cash after selling all 20 shares?
questions.explanation: Add $2,197.80 net sale proceeds to $7,998 remaining cash. Both fees reduce the final balance below the amount implied by the gross $200 price gain.

questions.prompt: What is net account gain across the complete purchase and sale?
questions.explanation: Subtract original $10,000 cash from the $10,195.80 final balance. The $200 gross price gain is reduced by $2 entry and $2.20 exit fees.

questions.prompt: What is net return measured against the original account equity?
questions.explanation: Divide the $195.80 net gain by $10,000 starting equity. The share quote rose 10%, but only part of the account was invested and fees reduced the gain.

capturedPayload.reflection: Write a three-line ledger for cash, holding value and total equity.
capturedPayload.reflectionGuide: Check that cash plus marked holdings equals equity. Keep the fee as an expense already deducted from cash; deducting it a second time from equity would also be an error.

capturedPayload.title: An affordable quantity still needs fee room

visual.caption: Hypothetical case inputs — not a live market chart

capturedPayload.scenario:
A virtual account has exactly $1,000 cash and an asset quote of $100 per unit. A learner tries to buy ten units because ten times $100 is $1,000. Apply the simulator’s 0.1% purchase fee. For this worksheet consider whole-unit alternatives only; the actual supported quantity precision depends on the instrument.

Compare buying nine whole units with attempting ten. The quote stays $100 and the transaction fee is paid in cash. For a separate mathematical check, allow fractional units with no rounding constraint and solve quantity times quote times 1.001 equal to the $1,000 cash balance. The computed upper bound is a worksheet limit; actual quantity precision and validation can require rounding down.

questions.prompt: What would ten units cost including the fee?
questions.explanation: Ten units have a $1,000 notional, and 0.1% adds $1. The total exceeds available cash. A displayed balance that exactly matches notional does not leave room for a fee.

questions.prompt: Which stated whole-unit alternative fits the cash balance?
options: Nine units, costing $900.90
Ten units, costing $1,001
Eleven units, costing $1,101.10
questions.explanation: Nine units cost $900 plus $0.90 fee, or $900.90. The remaining $99.10 is cash. Checking the full debit is more reliable than checking notional alone.

questions.prompt: What should an insufficient-cash message lead you to inspect first?
options: Quantity, current quote and the total debit
Whether the asset must rise tomorrow
Whether fees can be ignored in a simulator
questions.explanation: Affordability depends on the current price, requested quantity and applicable costs. It is an execution constraint, not a signal about direction. Reducing a quantity should follow a budget check rather than a forecast.

questions.prompt: What is the fee on the attempted ten-unit $1,000 purchase?
questions.explanation: Multiply $1,000 notional by 0.001 to obtain a $1 fee. Spending the entire cash balance on notional leaves no room for this separate charge.

questions.prompt: What cash shortfall does the ten-unit order create?
questions.explanation: Total debit would be $1,001 against only $1,000 available. The $1 difference explains the failure without implying any missing price data.

questions.prompt: What does nine units cost including the stated fee?
questions.explanation: Nine units at $100 give $900 notional and a $0.90 fee. The total is $900.90, so this whole-unit alternative fits the cash balance.

questions.prompt: How much cash remains after the nine-unit purchase?
questions.explanation: Subtract the $900.90 debit from $1,000 cash. The remaining $99.10 accounts for both the holding’s purchase value and its transaction fee.

questions.prompt: What is the fee-inclusive cost per unit at this unchanged quote?
questions.explanation: Apply the 1.001 purchase-cost multiplier to $100 per unit. This $100.10 is cash spent per unit under the fee rule, not the asset’s new market quote.

questions.prompt: Without rounding constraints, what quantity just fits $1,000, approximately?
options: 9.99001 units
10 units
9.9 units
questions.explanation: Divide $1,000 by $100 times 1.001. Actual execution precision may require rounding this mathematical upper bound downward so the debit cannot exceed available cash.

questions.prompt: Which action addresses the stated insufficient-cash cause?
options: Repeatedly refresh until cash increases
Treat the fee as extra shares
Reduce quantity to leave room for the fee
questions.explanation: Adjusting quantity changes notional and its proportional fee. Refreshing a page does not create cash, and the fee does not add a holding.

capturedPayload.reflection: Draft a pre-click affordability check in your own words.
capturedPayload.reflectionGuide: Use quantity × current quote, add the stated purchase fee, and compare the full amount with available cash. Leave room for a changing quote; do not assume a future fill must use an earlier display.

capturedPayload.scenario:
One hypothetical page quotes an asset at 100 US dollars, another at 92 euros. For this worksheet assume one euro equals 1.10 US dollars at the same time. questions.prompt: What is €92 expressed in dollars at the stated exchange rate?
questions.explanation: Multiply €92 by $1.10 per euro to get $101.20. The currency units matter: dividing by 1.10 would use the opposite conversion and answer a different question.

questions.prompt: What dollar difference separates the converted quote from $100?
questions.explanation: The converted €92 quote is $101.20, so it is $1.20 above $100. Comparing the raw 92 and 100 without currency labels would suggest an $8 gap that is not this common-unit difference.

questions.prompt: What remains necessary for a reliable cross-site comparison?

Ignoring conversion because both are prices
Matched timestamps and source definitions
questions.explanation: Currency conversion resolves one mismatch only. Different observation times, venue inputs or asset identifiers can still affect the comparison. A fair audit records these fields rather than declaring accuracy from one converted pair.

questions.prompt: At $1.10 per euro, what is the $100 quote worth in euros, approximately?
questions.explanation: Divide $100 by $1.10 per euro. The euro value is approximately €90.91; multiplying instead would reverse the conversion direction.

questions.prompt: At the original rate, what percentage premium does the €92 quote have over $100?
questions.explanation: The euro quote converts to $101.20, a $1.20 premium. Divide that gap by the $100 comparison price to obtain 1.2%.

questions.prompt: In the separate $1.08-per-euro branch, what is €92 in dollars?

questions.prompt: In that alternative-rate branch, how does the converted quote compare with $100?

It is $0.64 lower
It is $1.20 higher

questions.prompt: What dollar-per-euro rate would make €92 equal $100, approximately?
options: $1.08696 per euro
$0.92 per euro
$1.20 per euro

questions.prompt: Can changing the conversion rate prove the underlying euro asset price changed?
options: Yes; every dollar conversion change is an asset trade
Yes; conversion automatically changes units owned
No; the euro quote was held fixed in this branch

questions.prompt: Which record makes the price comparison reproducible across currencies?

Only the larger displayed number

visual.caption: Hypothetical case inputs — not a live market chart

capturedPayload.scenario:
A worksheet lists a $100 planned loss and a $300 planned gain per attempt. Four attempts produce the full $300 gain and six produce the full $100 loss. Costs are excluded. First calculate this deliberately fixed-payoff sample, then ask what happens if real exits fail to match the plan.

Compare a second payoff branch where the four winning attempts earn only $200 each while the six losses remain $100 each. Then charge a hypothetical $5 cost per attempt to each branch. These fixed samples illustrate how actual payoffs and costs matter; they do not demonstrate a repeatable trading edge. Keep planned gain, realized gain and sample net result separate.

questions.prompt: What gross total do four full winners contribute?
questions.explanation: Four winners times $300 each equal $1,200. This assumes every listed winner realizes the entire planned payoff. An intended target alone does not establish what a position actually returns.

questions.prompt: What is the net sample result after six full losses, before costs?
questions.explanation: Six losses total $600. Subtract $600 from the $1,200 gains to obtain a $600 positive sample result. It is a calculation for these exact outcomes, not proof that future attempts will match them.

questions.prompt: What would invalidate using this sample as a general profit promise?
options: Nothing; the planned ratio ensures profit
Different realized payoffs, outcomes or costs
Only a different chart color
questions.explanation: Actual win frequency, average realized gains, average losses and costs determine the result. Exits may differ from planned thresholds. A stated risk-to-reward ratio is not sufficient evidence of a profitable strategy.

questions.prompt: What is the recorded win rate across the ten original attempts?
questions.explanation: Four winning attempts divided by ten total attempts gives 40%. Win rate is a count-based measure and does not describe the size of each outcome.

questions.prompt: What gross loss do the six losing attempts contribute?
questions.explanation: Six losses of $100 each total $600. This loss must be subtracted from the winners’ $1,200 contribution in the original fixed-payoff sample.

questions.prompt: What is original average gross result per attempt?
questions.explanation: The original $600 gross sample gain divided by ten attempts is $60 each on average. It is a description of the sample rather than a forecast.

questions.prompt: With winners reduced to $200, what is the alternative gross sample gain?
questions.explanation: Four $200 winners contribute $800, and six $100 losses total $600. Subtract to obtain a $200 gross result in this separate branch.

questions.prompt: What total cost applies at $5 per attempt across ten attempts?
questions.explanation: Ten attempts each incur the specified $5 charge, giving $50 total. This conceptual fixed cost is separate from TradeHQ’s notional-based transaction fee.

questions.prompt: What net result remains in the $200-winner branch after those costs?
questions.explanation: Reduce the alternative $200 gross result by $50 costs. Changing realized winner size materially changes the sample outcome despite the same 40% win count.

questions.prompt: Why can’t the original planned payoff ratio guarantee the alternative result?
options: Realized exits and costs can differ from planned amounts
Every planned ratio executes automatically
A 40% win rate fixes all dollar results
questions.explanation: A plan specifies intended conditions, while actual outcomes determine realized profit. The alternative branch demonstrates that the same count can produce different net results.

capturedPayload.reflection: Which records would you need to evaluate the plan after use?
capturedPayload.reflectionGuide: Compare planned and realized exits, fees and each outcome over a stated sample. Include losses that exceeded the worksheet assumption and avoid selecting only attempts that fit the original targets.

capturedPayload.scenario:
A hypothetical asset once traded at $200 and now trades at $120. A learner calls it “40% off” and assumes it must return to $200. No evidence about business conditions or valuation is supplied. The previous quote is a historical reference; it does not independently establish fair value or the likelihood of recovery.

Consider ten units acquired at $120, with fees excluded. Compare a separate rise to $150 and a separate fall to $100, then the full recovery price of $200. The old high remains a reference, not a target guaranteed by the market. Express each branch relative to the $120 entry while keeping the earlier decline from $200 separate. A recovery percentage depends on the current base.

questions.prompt: What is the decline from $200 to $120?
questions.explanation: The decline is $80 divided by the original $200, or 40%. This measures a past price change. It does not show that the current asset is undervalued or that the earlier high was justified.

questions.prompt: What rise from $120 would restore $200, approximately?

questions.prompt: What conclusion does the earlier high alone support?

A guaranteed return to $200
A verified current bargain

capturedPayload.title: Selling half is not selling the gain

visual.caption: Hypothetical case inputs — not a live market chart

capturedPayload.scenario:
You own 10 hypothetical shares bought at $80 each. The current quote is $100 and you sell five shares. Ignore fees for the first two questions, then consider what fee tracking would change. The sale realizes a gain on the shares sold, while the unsold shares still carry an unrealized gain.

After the five-share sale, the remaining five shares fall to $90 each. Continue excluding fees to separate realized and unrealized results. No deposit or extra purchase occurs. Compare original $800 cost with sale cash plus remaining marked value. An observer calls the entire $500 sale receipt profit; identify recovered cost within that receipt. The later mark changes the unsold holding but cannot rewrite the completed sale’s price.

questions.prompt: How much gross cash arrives from the five-share sale?
questions.explanation: Five shares multiplied by the $100 sale price gives $500 proceeds. Proceeds include both recovery of original capital and profit; they are not the same thing as the realized gain.

questions.prompt: What is the gross realized gain on those five shares?
questions.explanation: The sold shares cost 5 × $80 = $400. Subtract this cost from $500 proceeds for a $100 gross realized gain. The other $100 price gain remains attached to the five unsold shares.

questions.prompt: How should a net-return review handle transaction fees?
options: Include applicable buy and sell fees once
Ignore fees because some shares remain
Subtract the full sale proceeds
questions.explanation: Net performance includes relevant transaction expenses. Record which fee belongs to which calculation and avoid double counting. Gross realized gain, remaining unrealized gain and net account return answer different questions.

questions.prompt: What original cost belongs to the five shares sold?
questions.explanation: Five shares bought at $80 each have $400 cost. Allocating the entire ten-share cost to the half-sale would distort the realized result.

questions.prompt: At the $100 quote, what unrealized gain remains in the unsold five shares?
questions.explanation: The unsold holding is worth $500 and cost $400 before fees. Its $100 gain remains unrealized because those five shares have not been sold.

questions.prompt: At the subsequent $90 quote, what is the remaining marked value?
questions.explanation: Multiply five remaining shares by $90. The new $450 mark changes the unsold position, while the earlier $500 sale receipt remains part of cash.

questions.prompt: At $90, what unrealized gain remains against the unsold shares’ cost?
questions.explanation: Compare $450 current value with $400 remaining cost. There is still a $50 unrealized gain even though the quote fell after the partial sale.

questions.prompt: What is sale cash plus the final unsold holding’s value?
questions.explanation: Add the earlier $500 gross sale receipt to $450 remaining marked value. Compare this $950 combined amount with the original $800 total cost.

questions.prompt: What is total gross gain across sold and unsold shares at the end?
questions.explanation: The $100 realized gain and $50 remaining unrealized gain total $150. The same result follows from $950 combined value minus $800 original cost.

questions.prompt: Which part of the $500 sale receipt is recovered original cost?
questions.explanation: The five sold shares originally cost $400. Only the remaining $100 is gross realized gain; the full cash receipt includes returned investment principal.

capturedPayload.reflection: Why would calling the $500 proceeds “profit” distort your review?
capturedPayload.reflectionGuide: State the $400 original capital inside the proceeds and the $100 gross gain. Then separate the five shares still held; their marked gain has not become cash through this sale.

capturedPayload.title: A closed market can have a fresh fetch

visual.caption: Hypothetical case inputs — not a live market chart

capturedPayload.scenario:
A stock’s last eligible quote was observed on Friday afternoon. The page fetches that same observation on Sunday. No new stock trade is stated. Crypto on the page has a separate Sunday observation. The shared interface can therefore contain assets with different ages even when the page request itself is recent.

For precise age arithmetic, assume the stock observation occurred Friday at 16:00 and the page fetch happened Sunday at 16:00 in the same timezone. Crypto was observed Sunday at 15:58. Ignore holidays and unusual trading sessions; none is supplied. Compare observation ages and decide which labels are supported. A working server on Sunday can retrieve an older eligible stock mark without creating a new stock trade.

questions.prompt: Does a Sunday fetch prove the stock traded on Sunday?
options: Yes; all markets share crypto hours
No; it may return the earlier observation
Yes; every fetch creates a market trade
questions.explanation: Fetching data and observing a new market transaction are different events. The case explicitly supplies an earlier stock observation; a recent HTTP response must not be presented as evidence of Sunday stock trading.

questions.prompt: Should the stock inherit the crypto quote’s freshness label?
options: Yes; one fresh quote refreshes all holdings
No; freshness belongs to each observation
Yes; both are on one page
questions.explanation: Each asset has its own source and timestamp. A shared page or batch request does not make every observation equally recent. Per-asset freshness prevents a current crypto quote from hiding an older stock mark.

questions.prompt: What wording best describes this stock mark?
options: A guaranteed Sunday sale price
Last observed quote, with its Friday timestamp
Live Sunday stock tick
questions.explanation: The supplied timestamp gives readers evidence for the mark’s age. “Last observed” is precise without inventing a new transaction or promising an executable price during a different market session.

questions.prompt: How many hours old is the stock observation at the Sunday fetch?
options: 48 hours
24 hours
Zero hours
questions.explanation: Friday 16:00 to Sunday 16:00 spans two days, or 48 hours in this fixed-time worksheet. The fetch timestamp does not replace the observation timestamp.

questions.prompt: How old is the crypto observation at Sunday 16:00?
options: 48 hours
Zero minutes
Two minutes
questions.explanation: Subtract Sunday 15:58 from 16:00 to obtain two minutes. That age belongs to the crypto quote and cannot be assigned to the stock.

questions.prompt: Which phrase would misrepresent the stock data in this case?
options: Cached eligible stock mark
Stock price newly observed on Sunday at 16:00
Stock observation from Friday, retrieved Sunday
questions.explanation: No new stock observation is supplied on Sunday. Calling the mark newly observed would confuse a successful retrieval with the underlying market event.

questions.prompt: Does a 48-hour-old mark establish the stock’s next reopening price?
options: No; the reopening price is not supplied
Yes; a cached quote guarantees the next trade
Yes; the page fetch locks the stock price
questions.explanation: The prior eligible mark can support a labelled valuation, but it does not predict or guarantee the price at the next trading session.

questions.prompt: What extra information could affect whether Friday is the last eligible observation?
options: Only the crypto refresh rate
Only the browser’s battery level
The venue’s actual trading-session calendar and source rules
questions.explanation: Trading calendars and provider coverage determine which observations are eligible. The worksheet’s simplified timing should not be converted into a universal venue rule.

questions.prompt: Which timestamp may legitimately change on a Sunday cache retrieval?
options: The original stock trade date
The page’s fetch time
The original stock observation time
questions.explanation: A retrieval creates a new fetch timestamp. Preserving the older observation allows the interface to show the mark’s real age rather than falsely making it fresh.

questions.prompt: What is a defensible combined-account freshness description?
options: Mixed ages, with each holding’s observation shown
Every holding is real-time because one is recent
All assets share the newest crypto timestamp
questions.explanation: Different holdings can depend on different observation windows. Showing their individual ages avoids treating one fresh asset as evidence that the entire account has current prices.

capturedPayload.reflection: Explain how you would display mixed freshness in a portfolio.
capturedPayload.reflectionGuide: Use per-asset source and observation times, with a compact summary when any holdings are stale. Keep the fetch time available without presenting it as the market timestamp for every row.

capturedPayload.title: A high win rate can lose money

visual.caption: Hypothetical case inputs — not a live market chart

capturedPayload.scenario:
In ten hypothetical attempts, eight gain $10 each and two lose $60 each. Ignore fees. The learner highlights the 80% win rate and calls the method profitable. Counting wins answers one question; comparing the dollars won and lost answers another. Work through both before deciding what the sample demonstrates.

Now compare a separate sample with the same eight $10 winners but two $30 losses. Then introduce $1 of hypothetical cost per attempt to both samples. The winner count remains eight in either branch. Track total winnings, losses and costs so the changing outcome is explained by payoff sizes rather than a different win-rate headline.

questions.prompt: What is the total from the eight winners?
questions.explanation: Eight gains of $10 sum to $80. A count of profitable attempts does not tell you the total dollars earned unless the size of each outcome is included.

questions.prompt: What is the net result across all ten attempts?
questions.explanation: The two $60 losses total $120. Subtract $120 from $80 for a $40 loss. The 80% win rate is accurate, but it does not make the sample profitable.

questions.prompt: Which summary better explains performance than win rate alone?
options: Win frequency plus gain/loss sizes and costs
Only the largest winning streak
Only the number of green entries
questions.explanation: Frequency and magnitude must be considered together. Costs can further reduce net results. A useful review includes all outcomes rather than selecting a statistic that looks favorable while omitting the account impact.

questions.prompt: What dollar loss comes from the two original $60 losers?
questions.explanation: Two losing attempts at $60 each produce $120 in losses. Comparing this amount with $80 total winnings reveals why the high win rate is insufficient.

questions.prompt: What is average gross result per attempt in the original sample?
questions.explanation: The original sample loses $40 across ten attempts. Dividing by ten gives a −$4 average gross result, despite eight wins.

questions.prompt: What is the original average winner-to-loser magnitude ratio?
questions.explanation: A typical winner is $10 while a loser is $60. The 1:6 payoff-size ratio differs from the 8:2 count of winning and losing attempts.

questions.prompt: With two $30 losses instead, what is the alternative gross result?
questions.explanation: The eight winners still total $80, but the alternative losses total $60. Subtract losses to obtain a $20 gross gain at the same 80% win rate.

questions.prompt: What total cost applies at $1 per attempt in either ten-attempt sample?
questions.explanation: Charge the stated $1 for every attempt, including losses. Ten attempts therefore cost $10; counting only the eight winners would miss two charges.

questions.prompt: What is the alternative sample’s net result after those costs?
questions.explanation: Reduce its $20 gross gain by $10 costs. The sample remains positive, but its net result is smaller than the headline price-only result.

questions.prompt: Which factor changed performance while leaving the win rate unchanged?
options: The number of winning attempts
The percentage of winners
The average losing amount
questions.explanation: Both samples have eight wins and two losses. Reducing loser size changes net dollars even with an identical win-rate summary.

capturedPayload.reflection: Write a fair two-sentence review of this method’s sample.
capturedPayload.reflectionGuide: Report eight winners out of ten and the $40 gross loss. Explain that the two larger losses outweighed the small gains. Avoid claiming either future success or failure from this small hypothetical sample.

capturedPayload.title: One rumor is not three independent sources

visual.caption: Hypothetical case inputs — not a live market chart

capturedPayload.scenario:
Three hypothetical social posts repeat the same anonymous rumor about a company. All link back to the same original post, and none cites a company filing. Counting the reposts as independent confirmation exaggerates the evidence. Trace the source chain before using popularity as a reason for a simulated decision.

Draw the source chain as one anonymous origin feeding three reposts. Now suppose a fourth message repeats the same claim but provides no new source, while a separate company document is located but says nothing about the rumor. Trace which items add independent information and which merely repeat or fail to address the claim. A primary document’s existence alone is not confirmation of every allegation.

questions.prompt: How many original rumor sources are stated here?
options: Three
Four
One
questions.explanation: The three posts share one anonymous origin. Multiple repetitions can amplify visibility without adding independent evidence. The source chain matters more than the raw number of posts.

questions.prompt: What would be a stronger next verification step?
options: Count more reposts of the same rumor
Assume popularity confirms accuracy
Find a relevant primary statement or filing
questions.explanation: A primary record can provide attributable information to compare with the claim. It may confirm, contradict or leave the rumor unresolved. More copies of the same unsupported statement do not independently verify it.

questions.prompt: How should the claim be labelled while unresolved?
options: A confirmed company fact
A guaranteed catalyst
An unverified rumor with its source identified
questions.explanation: Labelling the uncertainty prevents an unattributed claim from being presented as established evidence. A price reaction or a large audience does not itself prove that the underlying statement is correct.

questions.prompt: How many independent stated rumor origins are there after the fourth repost?
options: Two
One
Four
questions.explanation: The fourth message still traces to the same anonymous origin. Repost count increases distribution without adding a new independent source for the claim.

questions.prompt: What does a company document silent on the rumor establish?
options: It does not by itself confirm or disprove the rumor
It automatically proves the rumor true
It proves every anonymous claim false
questions.explanation: A document that does not address the claim supplies no direct resolution. Its primary-source status does not make unrelated silence into confirmation.

questions.prompt: Which finding would directly improve verification of the specific claim?
options: A fifth repost of the same anonymous text
More reactions on the first post
Relevant attributable evidence addressing the allegation
questions.explanation: Verification improves when evidence addresses the actual allegation and can be traced to an accountable source. Popularity and repetition do not provide that link.

questions.prompt: Why is three reposts not equivalent to three independent confirmations?
options: Only the first person can ever publish evidence
They share the same underlying source
All reposts are necessarily false
questions.explanation: Dependence matters: the messages reproduce one origin rather than three separate observations. This does not prove falsity, but it prevents treating the count as corroboration.

questions.prompt: How should a unresolved claim appear in a practice journal?
options: Attributed and explicitly unverified
Presented as a confirmed company event
Removed from uncertainty notes because it is popular
questions.explanation: Attribution and an unresolved label preserve the difference between a claim and established information. That helps future review avoid treating repeated rumor as fact.

questions.prompt: Does the rumor’s popularity supply a probability of its truth in this case?
options: Yes; three shares imply 75% truth
Yes; more shares guarantee accuracy
No; no calibrated reliability evidence was given
questions.explanation: The supplied repost count has no calibrated relationship to truth. A probability would need a defensible method and relevant evidence beyond social repetition.

questions.prompt: Which source-note structure best preserves this chain?
options: Only the most-liked message saved
Origin, repost links and verification status recorded separately
Every repost labelled an independent original
questions.explanation: Keeping origin and distribution distinct exposes dependencies. Recording verification status also prevents later readers from assuming an unresolved claim was checked successfully.

capturedPayload.reflection: Draft an evidence note that does not spread the rumor as fact.
capturedPayload.reflectionGuide: Identify that the posts share an anonymous origin, record what primary evidence is missing, and state what would resolve the question. Avoid repeating the claim with confident language simply because others did.
